title: Ethics and Ownership
overview: This topic asks you to think like a computing professional. Paper 1 tests why professionals need ethics and codes of conduct (BCS, ACM/IEEE), the impact of acting ethically or unethically in a given scenario, why copyright legislation is needed, the differences between commercial software, shareware, freeware, open source and free software licences (and which suits a situation), and the applications and social, economic and environmental impact of artificial intelligence. Marks come from applying a principle to the scenario in the question, not from general statements.
syllabusPoints: Show understanding of the need for and purpose of ethics as a computing professional.
Show understanding of the need to act ethically, including the role of professional bodies such as the BCS and IEEE and their codes of conduct.
Show understanding of the impact of acting ethically or unethically in a given situation.
Show understanding of the need for copyright legislation.

Show understanding of the different types of software licensing (Free Software Foundation, Open Source Initiative, shareware and commercial software) and justify the use of a licence for a given situation.
Show understanding of Artificial Intelligence (AI), including its applications and its social, economic and environmental impact.

definitions.definition: The moral principles that guide a person, and the rules of conduct recognised in a particular profession.
A set of principles published by a professional body describing how its members are expected to behave.
Formal legal recognition of the ownership of a created and published original work, giving the owner control over how it is copied and used.
An agreement that gives the buyer permission to use software under stated conditions; the vendor keeps ownership.
Commercial software provided free of charge for a limited trial period, without the source code.
Software provided free of charge with no time limit, but without the source code.
Software provided with its source code, which users may use, modify, copy and distribute according to the licence (Open Source Initiative).
Open source software (Free Software Foundation) that users are free to use as they wish, under a copyleft licence.
A licence condition that if the software is modified, the modified source code must be made available to others under the same conditions.
The use of a computer or computer-controlled device to perform tasks normally associated with intelligent human behaviour.

sections.title: What ethics means for computing
content: Ethics can mean the moral principles that guide a person, or the rules of conduct recognised in a profession. Professional rules of conduct must reflect moral principles of right and wrong, which can be viewed from philosophical, religious, legal or pragmatic (common-sense) points of view. Computing professionals need ethics because the systems they build affect employers, clients and the public: software controls money, personal data, safety-critical equipment and communication for millions of people, so a careless or dishonest decision can cause serious harm.
bullets: Laws set the minimum standard; ethical codes go further, covering honesty, competence and responsibility to others.
Religious and cultural beliefs of colleagues and users must also be respected in the workplace.

sections.title: Professional bodies and codes of conduct
content: Any professional is expected to act ethically, and joining a professional organisation provides guidance through its code of conduct. The British Computer Society (BCS) code is organised under four headings: public interest; professional competence and integrity; duty to relevant authority; and duty to the profession. The IEEE-CS/ACM Software Engineering Code of Ethics sets out eight principles: Public (act consistently with the public interest), Client and employer (act in their best interests, consistent with the public interest), Product (meet the highest professional standards), Judgement (keep integrity and independence), Management (managers should promote an ethical approach), Profession (advance its integrity and reputation), Colleagues (be fair to and supportive of them) and Self (keep learning throughout one's career). The codes differ in detail but agree that the public interest is the key concern, that they state principles rather than detailed rules, that professionals must use their own judgement, and that they should seek advice when unsure.
bullets: Benefits of joining a professional body: guidance on ethical behaviour, recognition of competence, professional development and support if challenged.
Do not accept work you are not competent to do, and do not claim a level of competence you lack.
Documentation is stressed repeatedly in the codes because it records decisions, lets others maintain the software and shows the work met the specification.

examples.label: Applying the code: testing time is cut
examples.content:
Scenario: your manager halves the testing time on a client's payroll system to meet a deadline.
Product: an under-tested system may contain errors, so it will not meet professional standards.
Client and employer: the client could be harmed by wrong payments, and your employer's reputation could suffer.
Management: cutting testing is poor, unethical management.
Colleagues: the team is put under unrealistic pressure.
Judgement: you should raise your concern with the manager and, if ignored, seek advice. Keeping quiet and planning to 'fix it later in maintenance' would be unethical.

examples.label: Two-mark answer: why a manager should act ethically towards the team
examples.content:
Any two of:
So team members feel valued. (1)
To get the best work from the team. (1)
So the team works well together. (1)
So the team produces the best product for the client. (1)

sections.title: Acting for the public good
content: Codes of conduct refer to the health, safety and welfare of the public and to the public interest; the BCS asks members to have due regard for public health, privacy, security, wellbeing of others and the environment. Poor engineering has wasted huge sums of public money. The Ariane 5 rocket exploded in 1996 because code converting a 64-bit floating-point number to a 16-bit integer overflowed. NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter failed because one team used imperial units while the rest used SI units. The UK's National Programme for IT in the NHS was scrapped after costing about £12 billion without producing a workable system. Applying the codes' requirements on specification, testing and project management could have prevented such losses. Other public concerns involve the purpose or effect of systems: systems not secure against unauthorised access, organisations hiding security breaches, private communications stored for security services, social media carrying abusive or illegal content, and powerful companies pressuring others to use their products.
bullets: Acting ethically: protects users and the public, produces reliable software, maintains trust in the employer and the profession.
Acting unethically: can cause financial loss, harm to users, legal action, loss of reputation and loss of the professional's job or membership.
Public attitudes to some issues vary, which makes individual judgement difficult, and whistle-blowers can suffer serious personal consequences.

sections.title: Ownership and copyright
content: Copyright is formal recognition of ownership of an original, published work. The creator owns it, unless they created it while working for an organisation, in which case the organisation can claim copyright. Copyright cannot protect an idea, only its expression, and cannot be claimed for material previously published by someone else. It applies to written works, music, films, recordings, broadcasts, art and computer programs. Copyright legislation is needed for two reasons: creating the work took time, effort and originality, so the owner should be able to earn from it; and it is unfair for others to copy the work and profit from it without paying the creator. Laws differ between countries, but international agreements mean the protection cannot be avoided by publishing in another country. In the UK the relevant law is the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act, under which copyright applies automatically when the work is created.
bullets: Copyright laws typically define how long copyright lasts, what happens when the owner dies, how copyright is indicated (e.g. the © symbol) and may record the date of creation.
The owner can state how the work may be used, for example 'may be published unchanged as long as it carries this copyright notice'.
A buyer of a copyrighted product may normally make copies only for their own use.
Distributing a copyrighted work, for example posting it online, without the owner's permission breaks the law.

sections.title: Software licensing
content: When you buy software you do not own it: the vendor keeps ownership and you pay for a licence to use it under stated conditions, and the source code is not provided. Commercial software is sold for profit, with options such as a fee per copy, a site licence allowing a set number of copies to run at once, or special rates for education. A vendor may also give away licences: shareware is commercial software offered free for a limited trial period (possibly a limited version, or a beta test version), and freeware is free with no time limit (often a limited or older version); neither includes the source code. The Open Source Initiative makes open source software available, normally free of charge, with the source code, so users may use, modify, copy and distribute it under the licence terms; its philosophy is collaborative development. The Free Software Foundation believes users should be free to use software however they wish. Its software is also open source and may carry a small fee to cover distribution; its licence includes copyleft, so any modified version must be released with its source code under the same conditions.
bullets: Commercial software is justified when it provides exactly the functionality needed immediately, works with software already installed, or comes with continuous maintenance and support.
Shareware lets users try before buying and suggest improvements; freeware may be enough for limited needs.

Open source or free software is justified when full functionality is available at little or no cost, when a few changes to the source code would make it suitable, when developers are collaborating on a new product, or when the user wants to control the software's future development.
Only open source and free software provide the source code.

examples.label: Which licences allow what?
examples.content:
User can edit the source code → Free Software Foundation, Open Source Initiative
Source code is provided → Free Software Foundation, Open Source Initiative
Free only for a trial period → shareware
User must pay to keep using it and cannot see the source → commercial
Modified versions must be shared under the same terms → Free Software Foundation (copyleft)

sections.title: Artificial intelligence
content: AI is the use of a computer or computer-controlled device to perform tasks normally associated with intelligent human behaviour. Applications can be grouped by the human behaviour they imitate. Problem solving: game-playing programs such as chess, and expert systems for medical diagnosis, which hold more knowledge than one doctor but cannot handle situations outside their rules creatively. Linguistics: voice recognition and speech synthesis, such as automated telephone help lines. Perception: autonomous robots and driverless cars that use sensors to decide what to do, rather than repeating fixed tasks regardless of what happens. Reasoning: drawing conclusions from evidence, for example proving mathematical theorems or checking that software meets its specification. Learning: machine learning, where a system improves its performance with experience by applying statistical algorithms to very large data sets, for example recommending products or filtering spam.
bullets: Social impact: more leisure and less dangerous or repetitive work, but job losses in some areas, new skills needed, safety worries about driverless vehicles, uncertain consequences if expert systems replace doctors and nurses, and huge amounts of personal data collected by global organisations.

Economic impact: new jobs manufacturing, installing and servicing AI systems and greater productivity, but fewer jobs where machines do the work, and a risk that the rich get richer and the poor get poorer.

Environmental impact: robots can work in environments dangerous to humans and AI can optimise energy use, but manufacturing robots uses limited raw materials and disposing of them adds to electronic waste.
If the data collected are not stored securely they could be used for criminal activity.

examples.label: Three-mark answer: how a computer uses AI to play a board game
examples.content:
Any three of:
The rules, past games and decision-making algorithms are stored. (1)
The program is trained by playing many games. (1)
It looks ahead at possible moves and chooses the one most likely to succeed. (1)
It stores whether each choice led to a good or bad result. (1)
It changes future choices, learning from its mistakes. (1)

comparisonTable.title: Types of software licence
rows: Paid (per copy, site licence or educational rate)
Vendor keeps ownership; use limited by the licence
Must pay to continue after the trial
Often a limited or older version
May use, modify, copy and distribute under the licence
Copyleft: modified versions must be shared under the same terms

diagram.title: Making an ethical decision
nodes: Identify the issue in the scenario
Check it against each principle of the code
Use your own judgement and seek advice if unsure
Act, and raise the concern again if it is ignored

analysisChains.title: Releasing software with known faults to meet a deadline
steps: The deadline is met and the employer avoids a late-delivery penalty
But the client receives a product that does not meet professional standards
Faults may cause financial loss or harm to users
The employer's reputation and the trust placed in the profession are damaged
analysisChains.evaluation: The short-term gain rarely outweighs the harm; the ethical course is to report the risk honestly so the client and employer can make an informed decision.

analysisChains.title: Choosing open source software for a school
steps: The software and its source code are free, so licence costs are saved
The school's technician can modify it to suit local needs
Improvements can be shared with other schools
But there may be no guaranteed support, so the school relies on its own skills or the community
analysisChains.evaluation: Open source suits organisations with technical staff and tight budgets; if guaranteed support is essential, a commercial licence may be worth the cost.

analysisChains.title: Introducing driverless delivery vehicles
steps: Perception and machine learning let vehicles drive without a human
Delivery costs fall and vehicles can operate day and night
Driving jobs are lost, although new jobs are created in maintenance and software
Public concern about safety and accidents may slow adoption
analysisChains.evaluation: The economic benefits are real, but the social impact on employment and the need to prove safety must be managed for the change to be acceptable.

examTips: Apply each principle to the scenario given: name the principle (e.g. Product, Public) and explain its effect in that situation.
For 'impact of acting unethically', give consequences for different groups: users, client, employer, profession and the individual.
Learn which licences provide source code (only open source and free software) and which have time limits (shareware).
When describing AI's impact, cover social, economic and environmental effects with a benefit and a drawback for each.
Use the full name of the UK law if you mention it: the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act.
commonMistakes: Confusing freeware (free, no source code) with free software (source code provided, copyleft).
Saying shareware is free for ever; it is free only for a trial period.
Saying buying software makes you its owner; you buy a licence to use it.
Saying copyright protects ideas; it protects the expression of an idea.
Writing general statements about ethics without linking them to the scenario.
Describing AI only as robots, without the other areas such as expert systems, language and machine learning.

quickRecall.question: Why should a computing professional join a professional body?
quickRecall.answer: It provides a code of conduct and guidance on ethical behaviour, recognition of competence, and support and professional development.

quickRecall.question: Name four of the eight principles in the IEEE-CS/ACM code.
quickRecall.answer: Any four of: Public, Client and employer, Product, Judgement, Management, Profession, Colleagues, Self.

quickRecall.question: What is the key concern shared by all professional codes of conduct?
Give two reasons copyright legislation is needed.
quickRecall.answer: The creator should be able to earn from the time and effort spent creating the work, and it is unfair for others to copy and profit from it without paying.

quickRecall.question: What is copyleft?
quickRecall.answer: A licence condition that modified versions of the software must be released with their source code under the same conditions.

quickRecall.question: What is the difference between shareware and freeware?
quickRecall.answer: Shareware is free only for a limited trial period; freeware is free with no time limit. Neither includes the source code.

quickRecall.question: Give three areas of AI application.
quickRecall.answer: Any three of: problem solving (games, expert systems), linguistics (voice recognition), perception (robots, driverless cars), reasoning (theorem proving), learning (machine learning).

quickRecall.question: What is machine learning?
quickRecall.answer: A system improving its performance at a task as it gains experience, by applying statistical algorithms to large data sets.
